A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VisioMath, with the same benchmark, construction pipeline and alignment strategies. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables and rendered figures support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations, option-shuffling experiments, error analysis and alignment-strategy results, including CoT fine-tuning.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds human and math-specialized model comparisons, similarity analyses and additional fine-tuning results.

M1.justification: The three strategies remain image concatenation, explicit option labels and alignment-oriented CoT fine-tuning. The caption-generation, refinement, filtering and shuffling pipeline in Appendix B is unchanged. Applying it to additional backbones does not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: The 1,800-problem mathematics benchmark and CoT training pool are unchanged. v4 adds an auxiliary top-5 diagram-retrieval scenario for evaluating visual encoders (Figure 4b), without expanding mathematical subjects, languages or source datasets.

E2.justification: v4 adds a human comparator and nine math-oriented model rows, including MM-PRM, MM-Eureka/CPGD and MathCoderVL variants (Tables 7–8). It also compares CLIP and BLIPv2 with Qwen embeddings in Figure 4b. All 42 earlier LMM comparators remain in the full appendix tables.

E3.justification: v4 adds mean/median-based similarity grouping, top-5 encoder retrieval, and strategy evaluations with Qwen2.5-VL-7B/72B and InternVL2.5-2B (Tables 4–5). These substantially extend the evaluation design. Existing zero-shot decoding, answer extraction and documented 3B training settings remain unchanged; human-testing procedures are unspecified.

E4.justification: v4 adds aggregation sensitivity and encoder-choice analyses, plus a recognition-error breakdown into four subtypes with four new cases (Appendix D.1, Figures 9–10). Strategy testing also extends across model sizes and families. The original shuffling experiment and four-way error analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point accuracies and error proportions without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new similarity aggregations assess evaluation sensitivity rather than uncertainty.

E6.justification: v4 adds human accuracy of 91.3%, nine specialist-model result rows, similarity-analysis results and recognition-error subtype proportions. Table 5 newly reports fine-tuned accuracies of 43.3%, 51.4% and 32.2% for Qwen7B, Qwen72B and InternVL2.5-2B. The earlier 42-model benchmark scores and 3B fine-tuning results are retained.

T1.justification: Equation 1 retains the same minimum pairwise cosine-similarity definition. The new aggregation and encoder discussion supplies empirical justification, without adding formal assumptions, mathematical derivations or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion retain the same claims: a visual-option mathematics benchmark, weaknesses under high similarity and image–text misalignment, and benefits from three alignment strategies. Additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations of human versus model failures, argues for the robustness of minimum similarity and suitability of Qwen embeddings, and gives more specific geometric-recognition diagnoses. The central misalignment explanation and K–12 applicability limitation remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-and-dataset access link in the abstract. It removes the GLM4.5V release-date entry previously given in Table 5. Hardware, software versions, existing training hyperparameters, data-generation details and prompt templates otherwise remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 4 removes the broad LMM/pretraining overview and adds comparisons with MMSciBench, SeePhys and VisAidMath concerning visual necessity and visual aids. References also expand for the new math-specialized baselines. The central positioning around comparative reasoning over diagrammatic options is retained.

P1.justification: v4 moves the single-image-model discussion to Appendix A.2, revises related-work paragraphs, adds Appendix D.1 and refines terminology. Affiliations, a corresponding-author note and acknowledgments are added. Most existing prose and the overall section structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds the two-panel similarity Figure 4, aggregation Table 4 and error-case Figures 9–10. Main benchmark tables are condensed and regrouped, appendix tables expand, and the fine-tuning table grows from one to four model rows. Existing error figures are relocated; these are substantive display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: Math-specialist comparisons and fine-tuning across four backbones strengthen evidence beyond v2's single-backbone training experiment. Similarity checks and finer error analysis improve diagnostic value. However, human results lack participant/protocol details, and new Table 4 introduces conflicting values: GLM4.5V minimum-similarity Q4 accuracy is 39.5%, versus 44.7% in retained Tables 3 and 8. These weaknesses limit the overall gain.
